standard.title: Complex and compound-complex sentences
standard.description: Understand how complex and compound-complex sentences can be used to elaborate, extend and explain ideas
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how embedded clauses can expand complex sentences to elaborate and explain ideas (AC9E6LA05). They have not yet worked with compound-complex sentences — the combination of coordination and subordination in a single sentence — or examined how sentence structure choices serve rhetorical purposes (elaborating, extending, explaining).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how complex and compound-complex sentences can be used to elaborate, extend and explain ideas.

nodes.label: Clause types and relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify independent and dependent clauses and explain the relationship between them in a complex sentence
nodes.minimum_width: Label the independent and dependent clauses in a given complex sentence; explain what the dependent clause adds to the independent clause
nodes.typical_width: Identify clause relationships across several complex sentences; explain how the dependent clause elaborates, extends or qualifies the main idea in each case
wider: Examine how the position of the dependent clause (before or after the independent clause) changes emphasis — 'Although it was raining, we went ahead' vs 'We went ahead, although it was raining'
Identify clause relationships in sentences from a range of text types (narrative, explanation, argument) and discuss how subordination serves different purposes in each
nodes.hinge_reason: Clause identification errors here propagate directly into Nodes 2 and 3 — students who cannot reliably distinguish independent from dependent clauses cannot identify compound-complex structure or explain elaboration/extension/explanation relationships.

response_modes.reason: Clause identification is a precision skill with a high error rate — students commonly mislabel the dependent clause as the main idea, or treat any long clause as 'complex'. Fluency here is the prerequisite for everything that follows; practice with varied sentence structures (not just textbook examples) builds the reliable recognition the later nodes depend on.

success_criteria: Correctly identifies the independent and dependent clause in a given complex sentence
Explains what the dependent clause contributes to the meaning of the sentence

nodes.label: Compound-complex sentence structure
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and construct compound-complex sentences, distinguishing them from complex sentences
nodes.minimum_width: Given a compound-complex sentence, identify its independent clauses and at least one dependent clause; explain how it differs from a complex sentence
nodes.typical_width: Construct compound-complex sentences by combining coordination and subordination; discuss how adding a second independent clause changes what the sentence can express compared to a complex sentence alone
wider: Compare a complex and compound-complex version of the same idea — 'When dinosaurs roamed the earth, vegetation depleted' vs 'When dinosaurs roamed the earth, weather patterns shifted significantly and as a result vegetation depleted' — and explain what the compound-complex version adds
Identify compound-complex sentences in published texts and discuss why the author chose that structure over a simpler alternative

response_modes.reason: Students commonly confuse compound-complex sentences with long or complicated sentences generally. The distinction between coordination and subordination — and what happens when both operate in the same sentence — only becomes clear when students see the structure across enough varied examples to isolate the pattern. A single textbook example produces surface recognition; breadth across sentence types and contexts builds the structural understanding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The comparison between complex and compound-complex versions of the same idea is genuinely rich — it foregrounds the structural choice as a meaning-making decision, not just a grammatical category. Advancing students can investigate how the second independent clause changes the rhetorical weight of the sentence.
success_criteria: Identifies the independent and dependent clauses in a compound-complex sentence
Distinguishes a compound-complex sentence from a complex sentence and explains the structural difference

nodes.label: Elaborating, extending and explaining
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how complex and compound-complex sentence structures are used to elaborate, extend and explain ideas
nodes.minimum_width: For a given sentence, identify whether the structure elaborates, extends or explains the main idea; give a reason
nodes.typical_width: Examine several sentences and match each to the purpose it serves (elaborating — adding detail; extending — adding a related idea; explaining — giving a reason or condition); discuss how the clause relationship signals the purpose
wider: Examine how the same base clause can be developed in different directions depending on the subordinating conjunction chosen — 'because', 'although', 'when', 'so that' each signal a different relationship and serve a different purpose
Compare how elaboration, extension and explanation are distributed differently across text types — argument texts tend toward explanation structures; narratives tend toward elaboration and extension

response_modes.reason: Students can correctly label clause types without being able to explain what purpose the structure serves. The elaboration/extension/explanation distinction requires students to reason about the semantic relationship between clauses, not just the grammatical label. An explicit reasoning scaffold — what does the dependent clause add, and what word signals that relationship — is what makes the distinction productive rather than a new set of labels to memorise.

The three purposes (elaborate, extend, explain) are not always cleanly distinct — a clause can extend and explain simultaneously. Seeing the structure across a range of text types and sentence examples helps students develop a flexible understanding of how clause relationships serve purpose, rather than treating the three categories as fixed boxes.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The relationship between subordinating conjunctions and semantic purpose is genuinely rich territory — advancing students can investigate how conjunction choice shapes meaning and begin to make deliberate structural choices in their own writing. This connects directly to AC9E7LY06 (creating texts for purpose).
success_criteria: Identifies whether a given complex or compound-complex sentence elaborates, extends or explains the main idea
Explains how the clause structure signals the purpose

nodes.label: Sentence structure as a deliberate choice
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can understand how writers choose between simple, complex and compound-complex sentences to serve different expressive purposes
nodes.minimum_width: Given a short passage, identify where the writer has used a complex or compound-complex sentence and explain why a simpler sentence would have been less effective at that point
nodes.typical_width: Examine how a writer varies sentence structure across a passage — when they choose simple sentences for impact and when they choose complex or compound-complex sentences to carry more meaning; discuss the cumulative effect
wider: Explore the ACARA elaboration insight that a simple sentence can express sophisticated ideas and a complex sentence need not express 'complex' ideas — find examples in published texts that challenge the assumption that longer = more sophisticated
Examine how writers use sentence structure variation for rhythm and reader engagement, not just logical development of ideas

response_modes.reason: The misconception that sentence sophistication equals sentence length is persistent and cuts across the whole descriptor. Students need to see enough counterexamples — powerful simple sentences alongside unwieldy complex ones — across varied text types before this understanding sticks. A single example is not enough to dislodge the length-equals-sophistication assumption.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: This is the integration node where grammatical understanding becomes a reader's and writer's tool. The insight that sentence structure is a deliberate choice — not a measure of difficulty — is the conceptual payoff of the whole descriptor. Advancing students who explore this across published texts build a transferable metalinguistic awareness that feeds directly into their own writing.
success_criteria: Identifies where a writer has used a complex or compound-complex sentence and gives a reason for the choice
Explains why varying sentence structure serves the text's purpose better than using one sentence type throughout
